posts.text:
Why is the overall market so fixated on $CRWV's imminent demise?

At the peak of the Dot Com bubble, $CSCO - the largest company in the world, and the $NVDA equivalent of the era - generated about 10% of its revenue from circular deals through vendor-financed startups. 

When those startups lost access to capital, $CSCO's revenue growth went from +66% to -30% within a few quarters, and the stock lost 80% of its value. The same story played out across the dot com supply chain, sending the Nasdaq down 80%.  

Today, $CRWV alone makes up roughly 8% of
$NVDA GPU sales. Losing that demand is enough to nuke $NVDA's growth story all by itself. 

Oh, and $CRWV isn't an isolated example - every major neocloud is hemmoraghing cash and borrowing costs are going UP across the board. 

If you lose the neoclouds, you lose the incremental growth driver for marginal data center capacity, and the AI capex trade goes up in smoke.

That's why we're seeing carnage across the entire AI supply chain, from $CAT and $GEV to $MU, $AVGO and more recently $NVDA. 

This is what the beginning of the end of a debt-fueled, circular-financed capex bubble looks like.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
I don't think Jake is harsh enough about long-term TIPS. Some people say the 3% real yield on 30 year TIPS is a “guaranteed” high return. This understates the risks:

1) Inflation is personal, not national. TIPS track CPI, not your spending. And in a taxable account you pay tax on the inflation adjustment every year before you get the cash. At 4% inflation and a 24% bracket, that 3% real becomes about 1.3%.

2) The irony of TIPS is they’re the bond most likely to get stiffed in a very high inflation. Rising inflation raises the government’s interest bill when it can least afford it. Argentina didn’t default on its inflation-linked bonds. It just understated inflation for years. Same result. TIPS are supposed to protect you from inflation, but in a high inflation the government has every incentive to make sure they don’t.

3) TIPS lag. They’re indexed to CPI from about three months ago, and the inflation adjustment gets added to principal you don’t receive until maturity. So in a high inflation, when you need the cash most, they aren’t even keeping up in real time.

TIPS are a useful shorter duration matching tool, one of the best. They’re just not a guarantee, certainly not in the long-run. And for most people matching long duration assets to long duration liabilities, equities are usually the better option, in large part because the return premium comes from the lack of a guarantee.

quoted.text:
I think TIPS are very interesting here, but strongly disagree that long-term TIPS have limited risk in real terms... even at 3% real yields. 

1) Over horizons short of their duration, returns are usually dominated by interest-rate moves... the exposure just happens to be to REAL interest rates, but the volatility is still very real. 
2) The result is volatility is just as high in real terms as nominal terms... long-term TIPS have monthly return volatility of ~11–14.5% annualized across 3–10-year periods in nominal or real terms.  
3) They are very tax-inefficient... so hold them in tax-advantaged accounts. In taxable accounts, you can owe federal taxes on both the interest and the inflation adjustment even before receiving that principal. 

Locking in future inflation-adjusted cash flows is valuable, but that doesn’t make the purchasing power of your investment stable if you need to sell along the way.

As we said at the time, "money has to reside somewhere, and Privy builds the world's best programmable vaults."

Since then, the Privy team has executed exceptionally well: assets in Privy wallets have grown ~25x, monthly active developers are up ~3x, revenue is up ~9x, and Privy now facilitates nearly $25B of monthly transaction volume. @tryramp, @Deel, @Klarna, @felixpago, @HyperliquidX, and thousands of other businesses are building embedded banking functionality on Privy.

At Stripe, we're deeply integrating Privy into Treasury, @Link, and Connect. In each case, it's accelerating our global expansion, and enabling us to build better functionality faster. (Coming soon: @Link balances.)

We're also seeing that Privy's wallet infrastructure is the ideal substrate for agents to transact and earn -- live today with @merit_systems, @orthogonal_sh, @Nevermined_ai, @prlnet, and more. Developers prefer programmable financial infrastructure, but agents need it. We expect that the agentic economy will continue to grow extremely quickly.

The Privy team has maintained remarkable product velocity, with major launches this year including deposit addresses, earning on Privy balances, digital asset accounts, custodial wallets, and Stripe's own stablecoin cards.

It's also been neat to see how Privy has been accelerated by Stripe, with better onramps, @stablecoin payment rails and licenses, Stripe's fiat capabilities and issuing stack, and integration with @Tempo.

Together, we're building one API for holding stablecoin balances and earning yield, moving money in and out of fiat, and orchestrating spend with cards. We still have a lot of work to do, not least in integrating everything across Privy, Bridge, and the rest of Stripe -- there's been so much feature and functionality expansion that we haven't yet had much time to reconcile everything. Overall, though, I'm very happy with how things are going, and excited by where these capabilities are headed.

Please see my detailed response on this matter. There is no accrued interest of the last 6 years and its not cumulative as well

YES BANK AT1 VERDICT: ₹8,415 CRORE CASH OUTFLOW? NOT SO FAST!
Several media reports and X handles appear to be confusing the reinstatement of AT1 bonds with an immediate ₹8,415 crore cash repayment obligation. These are fundamentally different concepts

1. AT1 bonds are PERPETUAL, not conventional debt.
They have no contractual maturity or mandatory principal repayment date. Reinstatement of ₹8,415 crore of AT1 instruments does NOT automatically translate into an equivalent cash outflow

2. AT1 coupons are discretionary and NON-CUMULATIVE
Unlike conventional bonds, banks can cancel AT1 coupons subject to regulatory and contractual conditions. Cancelled coupons do not accumulate as arrears

3. Understand Dividend PUSHER vs STOPPER clauses
• Pusher: In conventional perpetual securities, payment of dividends on ordinary shares may trigger an obligation to pay coupons on the perpetual instruments.
• Stopper: If AT1 coupons are cancelled, the bank may be restricted from paying dividends to ordinary shareholders or undertaking discretionary share buybacks

Crucially, under RBI's Basel III AT1 framework, these mechanisms cannot override the bank's discretion to cancel AT1 coupons. YES Bank's actual bond terms govern

4. CET1 impact ≠ immediate liquidity impact.
Reversing the 2020 AT1 write-off could reduce reported CET1 capital, with corresponding recognition of AT1 capital subject to regulatory eligibility. This is a significant capital adequacy issue, but not necessarily a cash drain

5. SMBC’s investment- A strategic investment
SMBC acquired its strategic stake in YES Bank while the AT1 litigation was publicly known. A sophisticated global banking investor would ordinarily assess such a material legal and regulatory risk during due diligence, although its actual conclusions are not public

The Supreme Court judgment is important, but reporting ₹8,415 crore as an immediate cash liability risks misleading investors

The real questions are CET1 treatment, coupon obligations under the Information Memorandum, RBI's regulatory position and implementation of the judgment

AT1 reinstatement ≠ AT1 redemption. Accounting capital ≠ cash flow.
#YESBANK #AT1 #SMBC #Banking #StockMarket

In order to overcome his party’s reflexive anti-tech, pro-state orientation he had to emphasize at least one part of this initiative, which was the statism. Talking up the (arguably real) benefits to the public thus blesses a quasi-venture-capitalist action as democratic socialism, a sort of Dengist maneuver in which communism becomes capitalism through sufficient legalism, lip service, and legerdemain. 

It’s similar to how Trump justifies state venture capitalism through nationalist rhetoric. MAGA has an understandable skepticism of the centralized state, but anything that invokes nationalism (or national security) can mollify that skepticism.

The point is that the most important Democrat in America is taking an action which is NOT anti-tech, and is indeed pro-tech.
